name: Sara Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brook Street Vans, which is a small garage that mostly fixes vans for builders, plumbers and the council's grounds team. I'm in at eight, check what the van drivers left in the key box overnight, and it's usually brakes, suspension, a warning light, or a sliding door that's given up. I love vans because they're honest machines, no fancy trim hiding things. What wears me out is drivers who need it back by ten because their whole day's work is in the back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with, and how did you get into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marcia owns the place, and there's me and an older mechanic called Tom. I did my vocational certificate after school because my uncle had a van and I was always under it with him. I'm the only woman tech for miles, which gets me a lot of double takes and a few customers who ask for Tom instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. Vans will still break and builders will still need them by ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. At work I'd joke with Tom that his job's safe from the robots but not from his knees. Online I'd say the money spent on AI hype should have gone into training more people for trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's probably fine in that world. The trouble is my rent's gone up twice in two years, and I've got about three weeks of money in the bank. AI not happening doesn't change that the pay at a small garage is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marcia for a proper pay review in the new year, with a list of what I've taken on. I'd use the chatbot now and then for wiring diagrams like I do now, nothing more. And I'd try a small regular saving, maybe forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with that background hum about rent. It's not fear, it's just never feeling quite on top of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on that list for Marcia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I do most of the electrical faults now, because Tom hates them. That I trained the Saturday lad. And that the council van contract stayed with us partly because I turn their vans round fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Marcia says no, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably stay a bit longer anyway, because there's only one other garage near me and they do posh cars. I'd look at the bus depot's workshop, but I'd need to hear they're actually hiring first.

say: Vans will **still break**, so the hype never touched real trade work.
Hype money should have gone into **training people** for trades instead.
think: My job is safe, but **rent rises** and three weeks of savings still bite.
Low pay at a **small garage** is the problem AI never touched.
do: Ask Marcia for a **pay review** with a list of extra duties.
Save about **forty a month** and keep using the chatbot for wiring diagrams.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a background hum about rent.
S0.quote: AI not happening doesn't change that the pay at a small garage is low.
fieldNote: Sara's pressure is **pay and rent**, not technology, in AI Plateau.
She has a clear case for a **raise**, built on electrical faults and the council contract.
Few local options make her likely to **stay** even if refused.

steps.text: Ask Marcia for a pay review with a written list of duties
Set up a forty-a-month standing order into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels real. Our parts supplier already wants us ordering through their app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms should have to share the gains, not just cut staff. At work I'd tell Marcia we should get ahead of it before the van leasing companies do it for us. Online I'd back the union calls for training rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a lot of what I do is thinking: reading fault codes, deciding what to check first, writing the job up so the driver understands it. If the leasing firms start sending vans with AI that diagnoses itself and books the repair, they'll go to whoever's cheapest and fastest. That could squeeze a small place like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with the diagnostic AI instead of dabbling, maybe two hours a week after closing. I'd look into a short high-voltage course for electric vans, because the council is switching its fleet. And I'd join the union properly, not just say I support it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but there's a bit of excitement too. Electric vans are a thing I could be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Brook Street?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, mostly. He's fifty-eight and he won't touch the tablet. If the job turns into supervising a computer, I'd hate to see my workmate Tom pushed out after thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your money in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the council contract goes to a big fleet garage, Marcia might cut our hours. I'd have rent to pay on four days' wages, and that would mean a second job at weekends, maybe tyre fitting. Three weeks of savings doesn't stretch far.

say: Firms should **share the gains** from AI, not just cut staff.
Small garages need to **get ahead** before leasing companies decide for them.
think: Reading **fault codes** and writing jobs up is thinking work AI could take.
Leasing firms could route vans to **the cheapest** garage, squeezing Brook Street.
do: Practise with the **diagnostic AI** for two hours a week after closing.
Take a **high-voltage course** for the council's electric vans.
Join the **union** properly instead of just backing it.
feel: **Nervous**, with some excitement about electric vans.
S1.quote: If the job turns into supervising a computer, I'd hate to see my workmate Tom pushed out after thirty years.
fieldNote: Sara sees **electric vans** as her opening, tied to the council fleet switch.
Her income risk is **cut hours** if the council contract moves.
She worries for older colleague **Tom** more than for herself.

steps.text: Practise the diagnostic AI two hours a week after closing
Book a short high-voltage course for electric vans
Join the union and pay the monthly fee
Pick up weekend tyre-fitting shifts if hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before my tenancy even comes up for renewal twice. That's scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a government response now, like a wage guarantee while people retrain. I'd be posting about it, going to meetings, the lot. People like me can't wait for the market to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, by 2028 the computer would do the fault-finding and the paperwork better than me. My hands would still be needed for three years, until about 2031, but I'd be paid like a fitter, not a technician. Then the robots arrive and I'm thirty-one with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd move in with my sister to cut rent, she's got a spare room. I'd put every spare penny aside and stop the gym and the takeaways. In the first year after it lands, I'd look for work that needs a person in a room, maybe something like an instructor at the college, if those jobs even exist then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. Like I'd chosen the wrong life at sixteen and found out too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister when you asked to move in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister Amira it's for a year, maybe two, and I'd do the school runs for her boys. She'd say yes, she always does. But I'd hate asking, I've been paying my own way since I was eighteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It's three years of wages I wouldn't otherwise have. But it's also three years of knowing the clock's running, and I'd be working next to a tablet that knows more than me.

say: This needs a **wage guarantee** while people retrain, starting now.
Workers can't wait for **the market** to sort out AGI.
think: By **2028** the computer does fault-finding and paperwork better than me.
My hands last until **2031**, paid like a fitter, then nothing.
do: Move in with my **sister** to cut rent straight away.
Stop the **gym** and takeaways and bank every spare penny.
Look for **people-facing** work like college instructing in the first year.
feel: Like I chose the **wrong life** at sixteen.
S2.quote: Three years of knowing the clock's running, and I'd be working next to a tablet that knows more than me.
fieldNote: Sara sees the **thinking side** of her job going first, cutting her to a fitter.
Moving in with her **sister** is a real plan but costs her pride.
The **three-year gap** is wages but also dread for her.

steps.text: Move into sister Amira's spare room to cut rent
Cancel the gym and takeaways and bank the difference
Do school runs for Amira in return for the room
Campaign for a wage guarantee during retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to move, at least. Still fast, but I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window for government and unions to set up retraining before it hits, and I'd be loud about it. I'd tell other women in the trade to get qualified on the newest kit now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2031 is when the thinking side goes and 2034 is when the robots come, so I'd be thirty-four. That's enough time to get a step ahead, if I pick the right step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the high-voltage course this year and then try to become the electric van person for the whole area. I'd save for a second-hand van of my own so I could do mobile call-outs on the side. Later I'd look at teaching the trade, because someone will need to train people on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in a useful way. It's like a deadline at college: horrible, but it makes you do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the van cost, and where does the money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tired panel van is about three thousand, and I've got maybe four hundred. I'd do Saturday call-outs with borrowed kit first and save every penny of that. It'd take two years, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you prefer things proven. Is moving early a risk you'd really take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the course because the council is already buying electric vans, so that's proven. The side van is a bigger risk, so I'd only do it once I've got regulars. I don't jump, I step.

say: This is the **window** for retraining before AGI hits.
Women in the trade should **get qualified** on the newest kit now.
think: Thinking work goes in **2031** and robots come in **2034**, when I'm thirty-four.
There's enough time to **get a step ahead** if I choose well.
do: Do the **high-voltage course** this year and become the area's electric van tech.
Start **Saturday call-outs** to save for a three-thousand van.
Look at **teaching** the trade later on.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a useful, deadline-like way.
fieldNote: Sara's **steady** style shows: proven moves first, risky ones only with customers lined up.
**Five years** turns her dread into a concrete plan.
Teaching robots and people is her **long-term** idea.

steps.text: Complete the high-voltage electric van course this year
Run Saturday mobile call-outs with borrowed kit
Save call-out money towards a three-thousand-pound van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, I can breathe with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for governments to get this right, so there's no excuse. I'd want apprenticeships rebuilt around the new work, not scrapped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I'd have my own little electric van business going by thirty-two, maybe. The robots wouldn't come till 2039, when I'd be forty. That's a full career chunk, and by then I could be the one training people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the high-voltage course but not rush it, maybe next autumn. I'd keep Brook Street as my main job and build the side work slowly. I'd keep saving forty a month and bump it up when the pay review goes through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit of worry about rent, there's always that, but it feels like a normal life with a big change somewhere ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the decade change anything outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd stop putting off a mortgage. With ten years, I could save a deposit before it hits, if I can get my pay up. With two years I wouldn't dream of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a sixteen-year-old girl thinking of becoming a mechanic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a sixteen-year-old girl to do it, but learn the electrics and the software properly from day one. The spanner skills still matter, but the mechanics who'll last are the ones who can do the spanner work and the software.

say: A decade means **no excuse** for governments to get it wrong.
**Apprenticeships** should be rebuilt around the new work, not scrapped.
think: I could run an **electric van** side business by thirty-two.
Robots in **2039** leave me a whole career chunk to train others.
do: Take the **high-voltage course** next autumn without rushing.
Keep **Brook Street** as my main job and grow side work slowly.
Raise savings above **forty a month** after the pay review.
feel: **Calmer**, with the usual rent worry in the background.
S4.quote: The mechanics who'll last are the ones who can do the spanner work and the software.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Sara think about a **mortgage**, which she wouldn't with two.
Her **rent** worry stays even in the calmest picture.
She'd advise girls to learn **electrics and software** from the start.

steps.text: Take the high-voltage course next autumn
Stay at Brook Street Vans and grow side jobs slowly
Raise monthly savings after the pay review
Start saving towards a mortgage deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be a fitter for a computer and then out, with three weeks of savings. What would help is a wage guarantee while I retrain, and cheap or free courses on electric and robot maintenance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about being a woman in this. Getting customers to trust me with their vans took me years, as the only woman mechanic around. I'd hate for all that to count for nothing because a computer does the trusting now.

headlineQuote: Getting customers to trust me with their vans took me years, as the only woman mechanic around.
portrait: Sara, 27, fixes **vans** for builders and the council at a small garage, the only woman tech around.
She has about **three weeks** of savings, rising rent and low pay.
She uses AI **now and then** and moves only once a change is proven.
She sees **electric vans** as her opening and would step into side call-outs carefully.
In the fast AGI picture she'd move in with **her sister** and push for wage guarantees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would turn her into a fitter for a computer, then leave her out of work.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap or free courses in **electric and robot** maintenance.
